problem: RI.K.3 is connecting two individuals/events/ideas in a text; this lesson quietly drifts into cause-and-effect only. The teach example (sun is hot, plants need sun) and the caterpillar example mix loose 'relatedness' with causation, so the through-line of what 'connection' means is a little muddy for a 5-year-old.

Only 1 practice MCQ (vs. 5 in the siblings), so the kid gets almost no independent reps after instruction; the lesson also slightly overstuffs the teach slide with four parts at once before any practice.
the 'Your Turn' Leo item is really find-a-detail, not identify-a-reason-that-supports-a-point, so it drifts from the actual standard

Tries to teach too much for one K lesson — short vs long vowels AND Magic E AND 'every word needs a vowel' — yet the interactive only checks identifying a vowel in 'fish', so the harder concepts go unpracticed and may overwhelm
the Your Turn tests synonym/comprehension (which word means big) rather than the taught skill of USING a new word in a sentence
the Your Turn only asks to identify the problem (the middle), not to retell/sequence B-M-E, which is the real skill
the Your Turn answer 'Tears' is a noun/thing, not the kind of vivid feeling-word the lesson just modeled, so the item undercuts the teaching
teaches three text features but only tests one (TOC); no worked example, so it names parts more than it models using them to find info

The tip slide abruptly switches to a third affix (-ed) that was never taught in the teach slides and isn't practiced, so it crams in an unmodeled concept; the lesson teaches un-/-er but the tip muddies the focus
The example beat is filler ('use new words') rather than a modeled application, leaving the teaching a bit abstract

The teaching is thin and abstract — it tells kids what each part does but never models it on an actual story before the interactive, so there's no worked example bridging the explanation to the 'Your Turn'; a child weak on this would jump from definitions straight to application

The Your Turn distractors are weak: 'Dogs' vs 'Playing fetch'/'Training tricks' lets a kid pick the answer just by spotting the most-repeated noun rather than by synthesizing the big idea, so it under-tests the skill it just taught
the Your Turn asks for the main point, not the reasons that support it, so the guided practice tests main-idea rather than RI.2.8's actual skill
the Your Turn compares two kids talking about pets rather than two texts on a topic, and only asks for the similarity, never the contrast, so it doesn't model comparing two books
by nature it can't truly 'teach' year-long reading proficiency, so it leans motivational over skill-building
it's a grab-bag (silent letters + PH lumped together) and the tip is a study habit, not a transferable decoding skill
the proud/joyful/thrilled discrimination is too subtle for grade 2 and the 'correct' answer is debatable
It is pure term-labeling — the kid never sees a real stanza, scene, or chapter in context and never touches 'how each part builds on the one before,' which is the heart of RL.3.5

Standard is about connecting events/ideas (cause-effect, sequence, comparison) but the example only teaches cause-effect, then the Your Turn tests sequence ordering — a mismatch that leaves the modeled skill (cause-effect) untested and the tested skill (sequence) only briefly taught

The 'example' is an abstract three-step procedure (author's view / your view / compare) with no actual text to apply it to — it tells the strategy instead of modeling it on a real passage, weakening the bridge to the otherwise solid Your Turn

RI.3.10 is a range/stamina standard ('read and comprehend informational texts at the high end of the grade band') — it isn't a discrete skill, and the lesson papers over that by re-teaching main-idea/detail (RI.3.2) instead; also the correct answer 'Bats are amazing' is a vague title-feel answer that competes awkwardly with the more concrete distractors.
the 'from Latin' framing is decorative and never pays off; intro hook is hollow and the suffix set is a bit arbitrary

No modeled example slide ('Let's Try One') — it tells about dictionaries but never models an actual lookup, and the 'Your Turn' (how are words organized?) is a trivial recall question, so the kid never practices the real skill of finding/reading an entry
the 'example' step only tells about inferring and never works through a passage, so the skill is quizzed without first being modeled

No modeled example slide at all — it jumps from bare definitions straight to the kid's turn, so nothing demonstrates HOW to identify a form before they're asked to; poetry and prose are never shown, only drama.

Skips the modeled example, so the kid sees definitions and then is immediately tested; it also conflates 'voice' with point of view loosely and never distinguishes third-limited vs third-omniscient, which RL.4.6 actually targets.

Thin on the actual standard — RL.4.7 is about how a visual/oral presentation reflects specific text descriptions, but the lesson stays at a generic 'movies cut and add scenes' level and never models connecting a specific text moment to its visual realization.
It teaches reading-stamina study skills, not comprehension of complex text — it sidesteps what the standard is actually about
The inference half of the standard is asserted in a 3-word pill with no modeled example, and the Your Turn only tests literal recall
the lesson teaches compare/contrast and problem/solution but the modeled example demonstrates sequence — a structure barely introduced — so the teaching and the model are misaligned

the teaching stays abstract ('combine all information,' 'full picture') with no actual modeled example integrating two real sources, so the core RI.4.7 skill of synthesizing across forms is never demonstrated
no modeled example at all — it jumps from a thin teach on reasons/evidence straight to the kid's turn, so the link between a point, its reason, and its evidence is never shown in action
no worked example before the kid's turn — the integrate-two-texts skill is described abstractly in the teach/tip but never modeled, so the first time it's shown is the question itself

The intro/teach is thin and abstract ('use makes them yours', 'casual for chats') with only one concrete word total; a 4th grader gets little actual vocabulary or repeated modeling, so understanding stays shallow
Commas (half the title) appear only in the tip slide with no teach or practice; lesson is lopsided toward apostrophes

intro overpromises (periods, question marks, dialogue, titles) but only compound-sentence commas is actually taught and practiced; the quotation-mark half of the standard is mentioned once and never modeled or assessed
the Your Turn distractors (close your eyes, skip the pages) are too obviously wrong, so it tests almost no real understanding
